notes: Bracknell Forest has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. HMO licensing is run by the Public Protection Partnership.
research: Rests principally on a complete council-published enumeration of licence types. The licensing index lists every licence the council issues (alcohol, animal, caravan site, charitable collections, commercial, explosives, petroleum, scrap metal, taxi and private hire, weighbridge, roads and street works, scaffolding, environmental permits, cooling tower) and the only property or housing entry in the whole list is 'Houses in multiple occupation licence'. Because that page is an exhaustive index rather than a topic page, the absence of any selective or additional property licence is positive evidence, not merely absence of mention. The living-standards page describes the Public Protection Partnership's functions as 'enforcing Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMO) management standards', 'licensing of HMOs' and 'providing an advisory service within certain areas of the private rented sector'. That last phrase describes advisory scope, NOT a designated licensing area, and is a plausible false-positive trigger. The XML sitemap contains no occurrence of 'selective', though this is corroborative only since the same sitemap also omits the HMO licensing page. STRUCTURAL CAVEAT: HMO licensing is delivered by the Public Protection Partnership, a shared service with West Berkshire, whose site returns HTTP 403 to all automated access and could not be read; any scheme document would most naturally sit there. Intrinsic risk is low: Bracknell Forest is a small, low-deprivation borough with a limited private rented sector.

council: City of Bradford Metropolitan District Council
notes: Bradford has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. The council's 2026-27 fee list covers mandatory HMO licences only.
research: Unusually well evidenced. The eligibility page states a licence is required for HMOs 'occupied by five or more people, including children' and 'occupied by two or more households' - the mandatory s.55 and Prescribed Description Order 2018 test and nothing else, with no area, ward, street or designation referenced. DECISIVE: the current fee schedule 'HMO licence fees 2026-2027' prices only mandatory licences, banded purely by occupancy: 5-7 occupiers £1,625.05 total, 8-14 occupiers £1,706.32, 15+ occupiers £1,787.56, each split into an initial and a final fee. A live selective or additional designation would necessarily carry its own published fee under s.63 or s.87; there is none. The complete housing navigation was enumerated, 80 links, and every HMO page is mandatory-only: Houses in Multiple Occupation, What is an HMO?, Information for tenants, Register of HMO Licences, Do I need a HMO licence?, Applying for a HMO Licence, Standards and requirements, HMO licence fees 2026-2027. No selective licensing page exists in the housing tree or the business licensing tree. TRAP WARNING: Bradford is a large, deprived West Yorkshire district of exactly the profile that commonly does operate selective licensing, and several neighbouring authorities do, which makes it a high-risk false positive in scraped datasets and in general model recall. The council-published fee schedule is the strongest available disproof and is the citation of record. LIMITATION: the committee system returns HTTP 403 to automated access, so no committee-paper cross-check was possible.

notes: Braintree has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. A new licence costs £595 plus £445 on issue in 2026/27.
research: The licensing page states verbatim: 'If you own or are the landlord of a House in Multiple Occupation (HMO), you need a licence if it: is occupied by five or more persons living as more than one household; facilities such as bathroom, living room and kitchen are shared by the occupants.' The mandatory test only. The published 2026/27 fee table contains three lines and no others: new application £595.00, issue of licence £445.00 described as 'Maintenance and monitoring of licence fee. One off with up to 5 year life', and renewal £550.00. No selective or additional licence fee exists. Neither 'selective' nor 'additional licensing' appears on any page in the HMO section; pages 1 to 5 of the guide were checked programmatically. TRAP 1: the DEFINITION page describes an HMO as a property where 'there are three or more tenants who make up two or more households', and also covers s.257 converted blocks. That is the statutory DEFINITION of an HMO, not the licensing threshold. Automated extraction reading the definition page instead of the licensing page will wrongly infer a three-person additional licensing scheme. TRAP 2: the council's own URL slug contains a typographical error, 'occupatlon' spelled with a lowercase L rather than an i, so naive URL construction returns 404 and can cause automated checks to log this council as unverifiable when the page exists and is current.

notes: Brentwood has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. A new licence is £890 and a renewal £603.
research: Under 'Do you need a licence?' the council states verbatim: 'Yes, a property is classed as a large HMO if it is occupied by five or more persons and it is occupied by persons living in more than one single household, with at least one tenant paying rent. A group of friends sharing a house will not be classed as a single household for licensing purposes.' Only the mandatory large-HMO test is given. Published fees are new licence £890 and renewal £603, with no selective or additional fee line, and 'A licence is issued for a period of five years'. The strings 'selective' and 'additional licensing' were tested for programmatically on the rendered page and are both absent. A site-restricted search returned only mandatory-HMO material: the HMO page, licensing index, fees and charges, registers of licences, private housing, other licensing, premises licences, the online application form and a 'Mandatory HMO Licensing Checklist' PDF. TRAP: Brentwood publishes a leaflet titled 'Property licence - Landlords - do you need a property licence?'. The generic phrase 'property licence' in that title is precisely the string that leads aggregators to record a borough-wide property licensing scheme. That PDF is a compressed scan whose text layer could not be extracted, so its body was not read; however every readable council page confirms mandatory HMO licensing only, the council's own checklist is explicitly titled 'Mandatory HMO Licensing Checklist', and no designation notice exists on the domain.

notes: Broadland has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. Licensing is run jointly with South Norfolk; a 5-year licence is £835.88.
research: Broadland delivers regulatory services jointly with South Norfolk through a single shared website with district-specific fee pages. The Broadland-specific page lists the entire Broadland fee set and contains only mandatory HMO fees: 5-year licence for up to 5 lettings £835.88; additional fee for 6 lettings or more £38.91 per letting; renewal £835.88; licence changes £38.91. No selective or additional licensing fee exists for Broadland. The shared eligibility page states verbatim: 'You will need an HMO Licence when all the following apply to a property: there are five or more occupants; there is more than one household; occupants share facilities such as a kitchen, toilet or bathroom.' It adds 'Since 1st October 2018, a licence is needed for HMOs regardless of the number of floors in the property', a reference to the mandatory scheme extension, not a local designation. The HMO section comprises exactly six pages and neither 'selective' nor 'additional licensing' appears on any of them. TRAP 1: the section landing page recites the full statutory definition from 'sections 254 and 257 of the Housing Act 2004', including three-or-more-person HMOs and s.257 converted blocks; that is definition, not licensing scope. TRAP 2: the word 'Additional' appears in the Broadland fee table as 'Additional fee for 6 lettings or more', a per-letting surcharge on the mandatory licence, not an additional licensing scheme under s.56. This is a direct false-positive risk for keyword matching on fee tables. TRAP 3: because Broadland and South Norfolk share one domain, a scheme belonging to one district can be misattributed to the other; the fee page relied on here is explicitly the Broadland one.

notes: Bromley has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. Bromley's 2022 HMO planning rule is a planning control, not a licence.
research: Confirmed with an explicit and recent statement from the council itself, the strongest evidence in this batch. The landlord page states under 'HMO licensing': 'An HMO will require a licence from the local authority if it is: Occupied by 5 or more tenants, 4 or more if there is a live-in landlord, in 2 or more households; There is at least 1 kitchen, bathroom or toilet shared by the tenants.' Mandatory only; 'selective' and 'additional licensing' were tested for programmatically and are absent. DECISIVE: a council press release dated 25 March 2026 quotes Councillor Angela Page, Executive Councillor for Public Protection and Enforcement: 'It is important to be clear that the council cannot use HMO licensing to control where HMOs are situated, nor determine whether a property operates as an HMO.' The same release states: 'Already the council has used its planning powers in 2022 to ensure that all proposed HMOs require planning permission, using an Article 4 directive, and where HMOs are established mandatory licensing regulate the minimum standards of the property.' That is a contemporaneous, named-member confirmation that Bromley relies on mandatory licensing plus planning control and operates no discretionary designation. TRAP 1, high risk: Bromley's borough-wide Article 4 Direction made in 2022 removes permitted development rights for C3-to-C4 HMO conversions. It is planning control under the General Permitted Development Order, not a Housing Act 2004 designation. Because many London boroughs genuinely do run selective or additional licensing, Bromley's Article 4 is among the most common false positives in scraped London data. TRAP 2: the landlord page cites 'The Licensing and Management of Houses in Multiple Occupation (Additional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2007' for s.257 converted blocks; the word 'Additional' there refers to additional management provisions, not additional licensing under s.56.

notes: Bromsgrove has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households who share a kitchen or bathroom.
research: The council draws the definition and licensing distinction unusually clearly in its own words: 'Definition of an HMO: Any property which is occupied by at least 3 persons who are not members of the same household', followed immediately by 'To be a licensable HMO the property must be occupied by at least 5 persons who comprise of two or more households and share at least one basic amenity such as a bathroom or kitchen.' The page cross-refers to 'sections 254 to 259 of the Housing Act 2004' for the definition. Only the mandatory threshold is licensable. The strings 'selective' and 'additional licensing' were tested for programmatically and are absent. The related-pages list covers only inspections of HMOs, the public register, landlord fire risk assessment support, LACoRS fire safety guidance and Private Sector Housing contacts, with no designation or area-based scheme. A site-restricted search returned only mandatory-HMO material. TRAP: the '3 or more persons' definition sentence sits directly above the licensing sentence on the same page and is a likely source of scraped false positives suggesting a lowered, additional-licensing-style threshold. STRUCTURAL NOTE: Bromsgrove shares officers and some services with Redditch Borough Council, but publishes its own HMO licensing content on its own domain and it is mandatory-only.

notes: Broxbourne has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies. A licence costs £1,820, plus £159 per bedroom above five. If you own a converted block of flats here, ring the council to confirm.
research: The council states: 'A rented property is an HMO if the property is the tenant's only or main residence for the duration of the rental period, and either: there are five or more occupants who make up two or more households and share a kitchen bathroom or toilet; or it is a building that is converted into self-contained flats and the conversion did not meet the 1991 Building Regulation standards and more than one-third of the flats are let on short term tenancies.' The fee page lists a single licence product, £1,820 per property plus £159 for each bedroom over 5, paid as two £910 instalments, 'usually valid for 5 years'. There is no second fee line for a selective or additional licence, which a designated scheme would require. 'Selective' and 'additional licensing' are absent across the six-page HMO guide, all checked. IMPORTANT TRAP, the most consequential drafting issue found in this batch: the second limb quoted above is the s.257 converted-block description, and Broxbourne's page presents it as if it independently triggers a licence requirement. It does not. Mandatory licensing under the 2018 Prescribed Description Order catches only s.254 HMOs occupied by five or more persons in two or more households; s.257 converted blocks become licensable only where a council has made an additional licensing designation under s.56. This is a widespread council drafting shortcut, copying the statutory definition into the licensing criteria, and it is a strong false-positive generator because automated extraction reads it as direct evidence of an additional licensing scheme. No designation notice, consultation or committee decision was found anywhere on the domain, and the single-product fee schedule contradicts one existing. Recorded as no scheme, but note the council's own published wording overstates the requirement for converted blocks.

notes: Broxtowe has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. Broxtowe's HMO planning document is a planning rule, not a licence.
research: Confirmed by the council in its own committee papers. The business licence page states verbatim: 'If you rent out a house in multiple occupation (HMO) which is occupied by five or more people forming two or more households, you will require a licence from Broxtowe Borough Council. If granted, a licence will last up to five years.' Mandatory only; enforcement text cites s.72 and s.73 with no s.56 or Part 3 designation. The housing-side page (updated 21/05/2026) says 'HMO licensing scheme. Landlords must get a licence if the HMO has 5 or more unrelated people live in it who form 2 or more separate households'; note the bare phrase 'HMO licensing scheme' there is itself a false-positive risk for keyword scrapers. The council's own site search for 'selective licensing' returns 'No results found'; a search for 'additional licensing' returns only animal, alcohol and gambling licensing charges. DECISIVE: Broxtowe Cabinet, 21 July 2026, item 32.1 'Fit and Proper Person Policy - Private Sector Housing Licensing' (approved; policy created May 2026, next review July 2031). Its Scope section states: 'This policy applies to all properties requiring a licence under: Part 2 (HMO licensing). This policy would also be applicable to all properties requiring a licence under Part 3 (Selective Licensing) of the Housing Act 2004, if any such schemes are introduced.' The conditional 'if any such schemes are introduced' is a council-approved statement as at July 2026 that Broxtowe operates no Part 3 scheme. TRAP 1, high risk: the 'Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs) SPD' is a Supplementary Planning Document controlling HMO concentration through the planning system, together with related Article 4 material; planning, not licensing, and it dominates automated HMO searches of this domain. TRAP 2, high risk: Broxtowe adjoins Nottingham City Council, which does operate large discretionary licensing, and Beeston, Stapleford, Kimberley and Eastwood are frequently conflated with Greater Nottingham in scraped data. TECHNICAL: broxtowe.gov.uk serves navigation-only HTML to plain fetchers and needs full browser rendering; /sitemap.xml returns 404 while the working path is /sitemap.

notes: Buckinghamshire has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households. Fees start at £1,050 for a five-bedroom property.
research: Confirmed across the web estate, the statutory enforcement policy and the committee record. The canonical page states: 'A licence is required when a house in multiple occupation (HMO) is occupied by 5 or more persons in 2 or more households. On 1 October 2018 the scope of mandatory HMO licensing was extended. It now covers all HMOs with 5 or more persons, including, for example: flats; bungalows; two-storey properties.' 'Selective' and 'additional licens' were tested for programmatically and are absent. DECISIVE: the 39-page Housing Enforcement Policy was parsed in full and contains zero occurrences of 'selective', 'additional licensing', 'section 56', 'Part 3' or 'designation'. Its section 30 is headed 'Mandatory HMO Licence Enforcement'. A live discretionary scheme would necessarily appear in the statutory enforcement policy. Committee papers were searched: 'selective licensing' returns seven hits, all legacy Wycombe and Chiltern district papers dated 2003-2007 plus unrelated recent items; 'additional licensing' returns taxi unmet-demand surveys and Additional Restrictions Grant material. No designation report, consultation or cabinet decision. Fees are a single mandatory product: £500 non-refundable application fee, then £1,050 new or renewal for a 5-bedroom property, £1,575 through enforcement, £998 for landlord association members, £50 per additional bedroom. No selective or additional fee line. TRAP 1, high risk: the legacy district structure survives only as three administrative routes and three mandatory registers, 'View the Aylesbury Vale area HMO register', 'View the Chiltern and South Bucks area HMO register', 'View the Wycombe area HMO register'. These are s.232 mandatory registers, not evidence of three area-based designations, and 'area HMO register' is a strong false-positive trigger. TRAP 2: the Article 4 Directions page defines them purely as planning instruments and the current list of ten, including 'Four Ashes, High Wycombe' sealed 29 May 2024, contains zero mentions of HMO. RESIDUAL CAVEAT: a full-text crawl of every PDF in the pre-2020 legacy district committee archives was not performed, so an obscure historic designation cannot be mathematically excluded.

notes: UNVERIFIED: Bury's landlord pages show only the national mandatory HMO licence, and we found no sign of a selective or additional scheme. We could not fully search the council's website, so please check with Bury before relying on this.
research: Downgraded to unverified deliberately. The available evidence points to no scheme, but verification could not be made exhaustive and a confident negative is not justified for a high-stakes answer. WHAT WAS CONFIRMED: the HMO licence page sets out the mandatory test only, requiring a licence where the property 'is an entire house or flat which is let to three or more tenants who form two or more households' or 'is a house that's been converted entirely into bedsits', in each case subject to the occupancy test that 'five or more persons live at the property, including children' from 'two or more households' sharing a kitchen, bathroom or toilet. Fees are a single mandatory product: £685.50 base for up to 5 persons, £29.00 per additional letting unit, £66.00 multiple-application discount, £100.00 new licence holder consideration. No selective or additional licence fee. The complete private rented section was enumerated and contains only four sub-pages: Customers, Landlords, Landlord Forum and Private housing repairs. WHY THIS IS NOT ENOUGH: no keyword sweep of the domain was possible. bury.gov.uk serves an empty sitemap.xml with no URL entries; its on-site search ignores the query parameter entirely and returns the same unfiltered set of 2,541 results for any term, including a blank query; democracy.bury.gov.uk does not resolve and bury.moderngov.co.uk returns HTTP 403, so no committee cross-check was possible. The negative therefore rests solely on absence of mention within one small section, with no means of confirming that a selective licensing page does not exist elsewhere on the domain. TRAP 1: the 'three or more tenants who form two or more households' phrasing sits on the same page as the five-person occupancy test and reads out of context like a lowered threshold. TRAP 2: Bury is a Greater Manchester borough and several neighbours do operate selective licensing, which is both a known source of scraped false positives and a reason not to assert a negative on thin verification.

notes: Calderdale has no selective or additional licensing scheme. Only the national mandatory HMO licence applies, to homes shared by 5 or more people in 2 or more households who share a kitchen, bathroom or toilet.
research: The HMO page states that properties must be licensed if 'they are occupied by five or more people from two or more households; and there is a shared amenity, such as a kitchen, bathroom or toilet.' The mandatory test only; no ward, area, street or designation is mentioned. It confirms licensing 'is paid for in two stages' and warns that operating without a required licence carries penalties up to £30,000, prosecution, rent repayment orders or inclusion on the rogue landlords database, all mandatory-scheme consequences. The parent section contains only four items: the HMO page, fire safety for landlords, the lettings redress scheme and the housing enforcement policy. Unlike some councils in this batch, Calderdale's own site search is functional and was used: a search for 'selective licensing' returns no housing licensing results at all, only an unrelated land-charges page. TRAP, high risk and actively observed: third-party aggregators publish Calderdale selective licensing landing pages, including one titled 'Selective licensing in Calderdale: streets, fees, postcode check'. These rank in general search results and are a live false-positive source. When one was opened to trace its sourcing, its own body text concedes 'Calderdale does not currently list an active selective scheme', and the only Calderdale source it cites is the mandatory HMO page above. The scheme exists in the page title and URL only. This is precisely the failure mode where a URL and heading assert a scheme the underlying council evidence does not support. TECHNICAL: calderdale.gov.uk /v2/ URLs now 301-redirect to new.calderdale.gov.uk, so stale links return 404. LIMITATION: the Housing Enforcement Policy July 2023 PDF could not be text-extracted, so it was not possible to confirm from the policy document itself which Part 2 and Part 3 powers Calderdale has designated; the public pages and the working site search are consistent in showing none.
